what_it_does: Gamma-ray bursts are catastrophic cosmic explosions that emit intense radiation across multiple wavelengths simultaneously — from gamma rays to infrared light. Scientists use ground-based telescopes to observe these bursts, but gamma-ray detectors in orbit detect them first, and ground-based optical telescopes must reorient themselves in real-time to capture the burst before it fades. This coordination requires rapid calculations: the gamma-ray detector continuously refines its location estimate of the burst, and a control system must decide when and how often to send updates to the optical telescope to minimize the time between burst detection and the telescope pointing at the correct coordinates. This paper develops an optimization framework that models how location accuracy improves over time and determines the optimal strategy for feeding updates to telescope control systems.
